Chapter One: Understanding the Roots of Financial Beliefs
You know, every one of us carries around a set of beliefs about money—beliefs that are often invisible, but quietly influence just about every financial decision we make. Some people call this your “money blueprint.” It’s like a hidden script playing in the background, shaping your choices and your results long before you even realize it.
Think back for a moment. Picture a child growing up in a home where money feels like a constant source of stress. Maybe there are arguments about bills, or every purchase is weighed with worry because of a feeling that there’s never quite enough. Now, imagine another family where money is talked about openly, and it’s seen as a tool for opportunity and growth.
These early moments? They’re like seeds—quietly planted deep in your subconscious. Over the years, they grow into patterns. Some help you, while others can really hold you back.
And it’s not just family that shapes these beliefs. The world around us—friends, community, even what we see in the media—plays a big part too. Without even realizing it, we absorb messages about wealth and success. Ever hear phrases like “money doesn’t grow on trees” or “rich people are greedy”? Those words can stick, creating a connection between money and negativity that lasts well into adulthood.
That’s why so many of us end up repeating financial patterns, even when we want different results. Maybe you find it tough to save, or you always seem to overspend, or you shy away from investing—not because you don’t know better, but because your internal blueprint is set to a certain “temperature.” It’s just like a thermostat. No matter how hard you try, you’ll keep drifting back to what feels familiar—whether that’s abundance, or constant struggle.
So, what do you do about it? Well, the first step is simply recognizing that this blueprint exists. It’s like shining a light behind the walls to see how the wiring really works. Suddenly, your habits make more sense, and change becomes possible. Instead of letting old scripts drive you, you can start to question them—and even rewrite them.
If you’re ready to start, take a moment to reflect on your early memories about money. Ask yourself: What were the common attitudes about money in your family? Were there moments—good or bad—that really stuck with you? How did the people you looked up to talk about wealth, or risk, or financial success?
When you bring these patterns into the light, you’re laying the foundation for real change. Because the journey to financial freedom doesn’t start with the latest strategy or tip—it begins with an honest look at the beliefs that have been quietly steering your ship all along.
